Building a Community That Lasts: The Complete Guide

Guidelowob research

By lowob · 19 October 2026 · 14-minute read · Growth

A community that lasts is a group of people doing a job together, with a reason to return that does not depend on being paid. Most company communities fail one of three tests: they are audiences rather than groups whose members create value for each other, they were recruited with incentives that selected for people who leave, or they are measured by member count, which says little about either. This guide sets out the sequence lowob recommends, from naming what you have to measuring who is still there after the incentives stop, and points to the article that covers each stage in depth.

Why most communities do not last

Three findings explain most failures, and they come from different kinds of evidence.

Participation is unequal by nature. Jakob Nielsen's 2006 analysis of participation inequality described the 90-9-1 pattern: in most online communities about 90% of people read without contributing, 9% contribute occasionally and 1% produce most of the content. A 2014 observational study in the Journal of Medical Internet Research tested this in four digital health networks with 63,990 members. The top 1% wrote 74.7% of posts, the next 9% wrote 24.0% and the other 90% wrote 1.3%. Adding members mostly adds readers. A community lasts if its small active core lasts.

Newcomers leave fast unless someone responds. Kraut and colleagues' study of Usenet groups found 69% of newcomers left after their first day. By day 30, 31% of newcomers whose first post drew three or more replies were still participating, against 12% of those who got none. On English Wikipedia, Halfaker and colleagues found active editor numbers stopped growing in early 2007 and then declined, driven by falling retention of good-faith newcomers whose first edits were increasingly reverted. Groups that ignore or reject first contributions stop renewing themselves.

Incentives select for people who leave. In a study of nine major airdrops, Messias, Yaish and Livshits found up to 66% of tokens were sold soon after claiming in some cases, and concluded airdrops "may be necessary to attract users initially, but insufficient on their own". Two years after the Uniswap airdrop, Dune data showed 93% of recipients had sold all their UNI and about 98% had never voted in governance.

The field still counts heads. CMX's 2025 survey of 589 community professionals found the number of active members was the most used health metric, at 84%, and only 24% could confidently put a financial value on their community.

Stage 1: Name what you have

An audience receives. A customer transacts. A user engages with a product. A network participant, such as a developer, liquidity provider or node operator, makes a shared system more useful. A community member participates in a group whose value is partly created by other members. One person can be all of these, but the strategies differ.

The quickest test is the peer-value test: remove the company for a week and see whether members still help each other, share knowledge and organise. If activity stops, the company has an audience or a support channel. That is not a failure. The mistake is designing for one group while measuring another.

The test can also be run on data. Common Room's 2022 analysis of 141 communities (vendor research) found members replied to each other 28% of the time outside GitHub, against 13% for staff. Where staff answer everything, the community is a help desk.

Some companies should stop here: products that need onboarding and support more than peer relationships should invest in those. Our piece on audience vs community sets out the four groups, the "members return because" sentence and when not to build a community at all.

Stage 2: Give it a job

A community earns its keep by doing work the company would otherwise pay for. lowob's framework names five jobs:

JobWhat members doContribution measure
TestUse early builds, report bugs, give feedbackBugs found, release sign-offs
TeachAnswer questions, write guides, onboard newcomersShare of questions answered by members
ReferBring customers, partners or hiresReferred sign-ups and their conversion
BuildIntegrate, extend, ship on top of youIntegrations and plugins in use
GovernMake decisions with real consequencesParticipation by people who are not whales or the team

Pick one or two. A community asked to do all five does none of them well.

Governance needs particular care in crypto. A 2024 study of Aave, Compound, Lido and Uniswap found only about 5% of tokens were cast on a typical proposal and the top three or four holders could decide almost every vote. Counting the largest wallets measures concentration, not community.

The job also protects against platform risk. On 15 January 2026, X revoked API access for apps that paid users to post, and The Block reported the KAITO token fell 14.5% that day. Community is a job, not a number covers the design choices that follow from each job: channel, rituals, recognition and ownership of the record.

Silence is the correct response to no job. A community with nothing to do will do nothing, however many people are in it.

Stage 3: Recruit and run the first hundred

The first hundred community members are recruited, not attracted. Paul Graham's essay "Do Things That Don't Scale" makes the general point for start-ups: "The most common unscalable thing founders have to do at the start is to recruit users manually."

lowob splits this stage across two pieces.

The first hundred covers recruitment. List 30 names: potential customers, respected builders, operators and sharp critics. Ask each for judgment on a real decision rather than attention. Give those who say yes a job with an end date. Close the loop in public, so they can see what changed because of them. Ask each for the next name. Because participation is unequal, the aim is to get the people who will do most of the work into the first hundred.

Find your first 100 people who actually care covers operation. Define an active member by behaviour (answering a question, testing the product, creating a resource, returning over several weeks) rather than by joining. Write a narrow member thesis. Start with one recurring ritual, such as a weekly teardown or an integration clinic, and make sure every newcomer's first question gets answered, which is what the Kraut findings point to. Give members consequential roles, run a weekly member-health review and invite the next cohort only when the first is getting consistent value. Growth through density beats growth through size: Common Room found engagement rates of 2% to 12% across surfaces, highest in smaller communities.

Kraut and Resnick's Building Successful Online Communities (MIT Press) turns the research behind this stage into design claims on contribution and commitment.

For media businesses, the first hundred are the hundred readers whose job titles you would put in a sponsor deck. Membership is the job applies the same recruitment by name to paid membership, where the market is tight: the Reuters Institute's 2026 Digital News Report found 17% of people across 20 paywall-heavy markets paid for online news.

Stage 4: Design the spaces and staff them

Opening a Discord or Telegram is one of the fastest ways for a project to feel operational. The interface resembles a community before the relationships exist. Discord is not a community strategy. Neither is Telegram. argues for starting with the jobs members need the environment to do, then building a small architecture: a start-here space with rules and security warnings, read-only announcements, structured help, one or two discussion spaces, a contribute space and events.

Platform metrics help if read correctly. Discord's Server Insights tracks visitors, communicators who post, and the share of new members who return after a week, and suggests about 30% communicators as a healthy goal. These measure presence, not whether the job is getting done.

Staffing follows from the same logic. Community management vs social media management sets out why they are different jobs. Social media management is editorial: the company's voice on its accounts. Community management is hosting: members' voices in the company's spaces. Combining them by default means one gets neglected, and which one depends on the person's temperament rather than the company's needs. The resourcing gap is real: CMX found 17% of organisations had no one working full time on community, the highest share it had recorded.

Stage 5: Use incentives as acquisition costs

Incentives can overcome a cold start, distribute ownership and reward early users. They also redefine what participation means. If a project rewards transaction count, participants maximise transactions; if it rewards posting, they maximise posts. Airdrops can buy attention. They cannot buy belief. sets out the questions to answer before launching any incentive: the behaviour being rewarded, the durable value it creates, how it can be farmed and what happens when the reward ends.

The evidence on airdrops is consistent. Beyond the Messias and Dune findings above, Keyrock, a crypto market maker, reviewed 62 airdrops in 2024 and found only eight trading above their launch price after 90 days, with larger distributions holding up better than small ones.

Community that survives the airdrop turns this into a plan. Treat the airdrop as an acquisition cost with an expected sell-through. Weight allocation to repeated usage over time. Build sybil filters before the snapshot, publish the rules and keep an appeals channel a human reads. Give holders a job: test, curate, govern or refer.

Paid creators are the same problem in a different channel. KOL campaigns need more than impression screenshots argues for defining the action before buying placements and judging spend by cost per activated, retained user rather than reach. For the wider cost logic, see demand generation economics.

Stage 6: Measure contribution and retention

Member count is the easiest number to inflate and one of the weakest indicators of health. Replace it with measures that match the job and show whether people stay.

MeasureWhat it showsWhere it fits
Meaningful first contributions by newcomersWhether people move past readingEvery community
Time to a useful responseWhether newcomers are being answeredEvery community; critical in the first hundred
Share of questions answered by membersPeer value existsTeach job
Distinct contributors per monthBreadth of the active coreEvery community
Contribution to the chosen jobBugs, referrals, integrations, guidesTest, refer, build, teach
Governance participation excluding the largest holders and teamReal distribution of decisionsGovern job
Retained usage 30 days after incentives stopThe community that remainsAny incentive programme
Member retention and paid revenue from referring membersWhether peer value funds the businessMedia memberships

The single most important line is the retained-usage figure. Define the action that means someone is using the product, not visiting it. Run incentives for a set period, stop, and count how many keep doing it. Write the decision you will make on the result before you start; campaign testing that reaches a decision covers how. Keep that record (a member list, a contribution log and a way to reach people) on systems you own, so a platform policy change cannot take it.

When it has gone wrong

A large, silent group was usually recruited for a payout, lives on a rented platform and shares only an interest in price or launch news. Some silence is normal, but a large group with no active core has a design problem. "40,000 members and nobody does anything" sets out the turnaround: pick one job, hand-recruit thirty people from the channel history who asked real questions or helped others, ask them for judgment on a real decision, close the loop in public, switch incentives off for a month and count who stays. Do not buy more members or announce a token to wake the group up.

lowob takeaways

  • Name the group. Run the peer-value test before calling anything a community.
  • Assign one or two jobs. Test, teach, refer, build or govern, each with its own contribution measure.
  • Recruit the first hundred by hand. Ask for judgment, close the loop and answer every first contribution.
  • Design small and host it. A few spaces with clear jobs, run by a host rather than a publisher.
  • Cost the incentives. Airdrops, points and paid creators are acquisition spend with an expected loss rate.
  • Count who stays. Retained contribution after incentives stop is the community.
Gateway card

Before you call it a community

  • You can complete "members return because they can ___ with people they could not easily ___ elsewhere"
  • One or two named jobs, each with a contribution measure
  • A named first hundred, recruited by hand, with a record of each person's first contribution
  • One recurring ritual and a host responsible for answering newcomers
  • Every incentive costed, with a date it stops and a retained-usage count planned
  • Member records held on systems you own

Common questions

How do you build an online community that lasts?

Decide whether you need a community at all, give it one or two jobs, recruit the first hundred members by hand, run one recurring ritual, treat incentives as acquisition costs and measure who keeps contributing after the incentives stop.

What is the 90-9-1 rule?

Jakob Nielsen's observation that about 90% of community members only read, 9% contribute occasionally and 1% produce most content. A 2014 study of four health networks found the top 1% wrote about 75% of posts.

Do airdrops build community?

Rarely on their own. Studies of major airdrops find most recipients sell quickly; two years after Uniswap's, 93% of recipients had sold all their tokens. Airdrops can attract users, but a job and a reason to return are what keep them.

What metrics should a community team report?

Contribution to the community's job, newcomers' first contributions, time to a useful response, distinct contributors and retained usage after incentives stop. Member count alone says little about health or value.

Sources and notes

  • Nielsen Norman Group, Participation Inequality: The 90-9-1 Rule, 8 October 2006. Practitioner analysis; ratios are a rule of thumb.
  • van Mierlo, The 1% Rule in Four Digital Health Social Networks, Journal of Medical Internet Research, 4 February 2014. Peer-reviewed; 63,990 members of health networks.
  • Kraut, Wang, Butler, Joyce and Burke, Beyond Information: Developing the Relationship between the Individual and the Group in Online Communities, manuscript dated 18 April 2008. Working paper; Usenet groups; behavioural measures.
  • Kraut and Resnick, Building Successful Online Communities: Evidence-Based Social Design, MIT Press, paperback edition February 2016. Academic book; publisher description consulted.
  • Halfaker, Geiger, Morgan and Riedl, The Rise and Decline of an Open Collaboration System, summary on Wikimedia Meta, 2013. Published in American Behavioral Scientist; English Wikipedia only.
  • Paul Graham, Do Things That Don't Scale, July 2013. Founder essay.
  • CMX, 2025 Community Industry Report, 2025. Survey of 589 community professionals; CMX is owned by Bevy, a community software vendor; self-reported.
  • Common Room, 360: Community-Led Growth Report, 17 November 2022. Vendor research on 141 communities using Common Room.
  • Discord, Getting to Know Your Server With Server Insights, undated. Platform documentation.
  • Messias, Yaish and Livshits, Airdrops: Giving Money Away Is Harder Than It Seems, arXiv, revised July 2025. Academic preprint; nine airdrops.
  • Dune, The Uniswap Airdrop: Lessons for the Industry, late 2022. Community analysis on Dune's analytics platform; one airdrop.
  • Keyrock, Airdrops in the Barren Desert, 25 September 2024. Research by a crypto market maker; price performance of 62 airdrops.
  • Falk, Pathan, Rigas and Tsoukalas, Blockchain Governance: An Empirical Analysis of User Engagement on DAOs, arXiv, 15 July 2024. Preprint; four DeFi protocols.
  • The Block, Kaito token plummets after X revises API policies to ban InfoFi crypto projects, 15 January 2026. News report.
  • Reuters Institute, Digital News Report 2026: executive summary, 16 June 2026. Survey of 97,520 people in 48 markets.
